content: Japan's economy shrank in the July-September quarter, its first contraction in a year, as high prices squeezed household spending and weak exports dragged on growth, according to preliminary government data released on Monday. Real gross domestic product fell at an annualised rate of 0.1 percent in the third quarter, the Cabinet Office said, a result that fell short of what economists had expected and marked a sharp reversal from the 1.7 percent annualised expansion recorded in the April-June period. On a quarter-on-quarter basis, output was essentially flat, slipping 0.02 percent, against forecasts for a small gain. It was the first negative reading in four quarters, and it ended a run of three consecutive quarters of growth. The figures were weaker than the median forecast of economists surveyed by QUICK, a Nikkei group company, who had expected annualised growth of 0.2 percent, while a separate Reuters poll had pointed to 0.3 percent. The miss was not large in absolute terms, but it was enough to change the story of Japan's recovery. Instead of steady, if unspectacular, expansion, the world's fourth-largest economy spent the summer standing still. The main drag came from households. Private consumption, which accounts for more than half of Japan's economic output, fell 0.3 percent from the previous quarter, its second consecutive quarterly decline. Rising prices for food and energy have eaten into household budgets, and bad weather during the quarter kept shoppers at home, Kyodo News reported, citing the Cabinet Office data. Daiwa Institute of Research economist Hirohito Hatanaka said the sharper-than-expected drop in consumption weighed heavily on the overall result. Trade was the other weak spot. Exports slipped 0.2 percent in the quarter, and net external demand subtracted 0.6 percentage point from growth, a bigger drag than the 0.4 point economists had pencilled in. Inbound tourism consumption, which had been a bright spot in earlier quarters as visitors returned in large numbers, fell 2.4 percent. There were, however, signs of resilience beneath the headline. Business investment rose 1.6 percent from the previous quarter, beating forecasts of a 1.5 percent gain and recovering from a 0.9 percent drop in the second quarter. Domestic demand as a whole added 0.6 percentage point to growth. Industrial production also rebounded, rising 2.0 percent month on month in September after a 2.4 percent drop in August, according to separate data released on Monday. Nominal GDP, which is not adjusted for inflation, grew 0.4 percent from the previous quarter, or 1.6 percent on an annualised basis, suggesting the economy continued to generate income even as real output stalled. The GDP deflator, a broad measure of prices across the economy, rose 2.4 percent from a year earlier, still comfortably above the Bank of Japan's 2 percent target. On a year-on-year basis, the economy grew 1.1 percent, its strongest showing since the second quarter of 2025. The figures land at a sensitive moment for the Bank of Japan. The central bank held its policy rate at 1.25 percent in October and is widely expected to raise it to 1.5 percent in December, with market pricing putting the chance of a 25-basis-point increase at roughly three in four. A flat quarter driven mainly by trade is unlikely on its own to derail the tightening case, analysts said, particularly with business investment holding up and inflation still above target. Attention now turns to Bank of Japan board member Hajime Takata, who speaks later on Monday. Takata has dissented at recent policy meetings in favour of faster tightening, and his reading of the data will be watched closely for any shift in the December debate. Economists are divided on what the contraction means. Some see it as a temporary setback, with the Japan Center for Economic Research forecasting annualised growth of 0.67 percent in the October-December quarter, and projecting growth of 0.89 percent for fiscal 2026 and 1.02 percent for fiscal 2027. Others warn that two consecutive quarters of falling consumption point to a deeper problem: households are struggling with the cost of living, and the economy's recovery remains fragile. A revised estimate of third-quarter GDP is due next month, and it could change the picture if the consumption or investment figures are updated. For now, the data tell a simple story. Japan's economy did not fall off a cliff in the summer, but it stopped moving forward, and the households at its centre are feeling the strain.
summary: Japan's economy shrank at an annualised rate of 0.1 percent in the third quarter, its first contraction in four quarters, as high prices hit household spending and exports weakened, preliminary Cabinet Office data showed on Monday.
title: Japan's economy contracts in third quarter as spending and exports weaken
